article_title: Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment
citation: Aaron J. Peltoniemi, Joni Lämsä, Sami Lehesvuori, Raija Hämäläinen. (2025). Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09447-6
title: Dialogical self theory (DST) I-positions as a CSCL analytical framework
description: DST holds that, as the article states, "the self is populated by other inner selves that collectively derive from the world and have their own voice, motives, opinions, and knowledge that become present in what are known as I-positions via dialogue in response to the social situation". The article operationalizes four positions — I–it (objectified technological other), I–me (personal knowledge), I–you (encountered other), I–we (collective identity) — grounded at utterance level to visualize knowledge and identity construction in CSCL.
requirements: Discourse must be transcribed and divided into utterances so I-positions can be grounded individually and reviewed through intersubjectivity among researchers
constraints: I-positions in this study are a snapshot of the current state of polyphony at the timing of the learning task, not temporal trajectories
Notions of what constitutes the other within the dialogical self are not always clear, especially with digital technologies
target_learners: undergraduate physics students collaborating in small groups
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction through collaborative inquiry-based problem solving
examples: Four themes from Johnstone's grounding framework were merged onto the four I-positions, one theme per position, with descriptions and example utterances in Appendix Table 2
key_sources: Aaron J. Peltoniemi, Joni Lämsä, Sami Lehesvuori, Raija Hämäläinen. (2025). Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09447-6

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity (DSMRI): a two-level CDS model of motivated action
description: The DSMRI is a Complex Dynamic Systems model of identity, motivation, and action whose unit-of-analysis is the individual's situated role identity. It answers the question of why a particular person acts a particular way in a particular situation through two integrated levels: a sociocultural level, in which "a person generally acts according to the sociocultural role they occupy in a particular cultural activity system," and an individual level, in which different people in the same role construct idiosyncratic role identities as non-deterministic dynamic systems. Culture and individual are treated as two facets of a single emergent motivational phenomenon rather than independent construct sets. The model draws its sociocultural framing from Cultural-Historical Activity Theory and its individual-level content from Personal Investment Theory.
requirements: Requires conceptualizing the unit-of-analysis as the agent-within-her-sociocultural-situation rather than isolated individual constructs or activity structure alone
constraints: The article states the model's contribution is clarification of its conception of culture, not a comprehensive review of complexity theory or a catalog of motivational constructs
target_learning_goals: Understanding and explaining situated motivated action
Designing motivationally supportive educational environments
examples: The article uses the case of Maya, a high-achieving student who remains silent during a whole-class discussion of a contested historical event, to illustrate how the two levels integrate
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: Role identity content comprises four interdependent, partially overlapping conceptual categories
description: Building on Personal Investment Theory, the content of the role identity system comprises interdependent elements from four conceptual categories: ontological and epistemological beliefs, purpose and goals, self-perceptions and self-definitions, and perceived action possibilities, each with tied emotions. The article states that established motivational constructs are posited "as dynamic, situated and interdependent elements within this CDS rather than as independent predictors." The categories are not mutually exclusive—constructs such as self-efficacy lie at the intersection of multiple categories—and the particular construct salient within a component ebbs and flows across time, situations, and persons.
requirements: Each component comprises both role-related knowledge and the associated affect; emotion is the affect tied to all four components and their relations
constraints: The article notes the components' partial overlap means some established constructs are located at their intersections rather than within a single category
target_learners: Any agent occupying a sociocultural role
target_learning_goals: Explaining why a particular person acts a particular way in a particular situation
examples: Table 1 maps illustrative established constructs to each component, e.g., causal attributions and implicit theories under ontological and epistemological beliefs, achievement goal orientations under purpose and goals
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation
citation: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y
title: Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation (DSMDS)
description: DSMDS is an SDT-grounded conceptual framework that treats adolescent digital self-regulation as a developmental process rather than a problem of exposure control. The article states the model "conceptualizes digital self-regulation as a developmental process through which adolescents learn to navigate digital environments as their executive functions, motivational capacities, and social ecologies mature." It integrates two core components—digital literacy competence as the knowledge and meaning-making foundation, and regulatory strategies as the enactment layer—shaped by autonomy-supportive or controlling conditions across family, school, peer, and policy contexts. Internalization of regulation is hypothesized but treated as contingent rather than inevitable.
requirements: Requires consideration of adolescents' developing executive function and basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness
constraints: The article states the coordination framework "remains a conceptual proposition intended to organize future research rather than a settled empirical sequence in the digital-specific literature"
target_learning_goals: intentional, self-directed digital engagement
sustained attention and goal-directed technology use
digital literacy development
examples: The article presents Fig. 1 as a visual conceptualization of the model and applies it to devices, platforms, and activities including social media, gaming, messaging, and AI-based platforms
key_sources: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y

article_title: Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling
citation: Nicole M. Hutchins & Gautam Biswas & Ningyu Zhang & Caitlin Snyder & Ákos Lédeczi & Miklós Maróti. (2020). Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00209-z
title: Educational DSML design framework built on three principles: evidence-centered design, exploratory learning of dynamic processes, and a block-based programming environment
description: The article's design framework rests on three principles the authors name explicitly: "An evidence-centered design approach ... to ensure coherence and coverage of domain concepts, relations, and practices in the design of the DSML constructs"; opportunities "for exploratory learning of dynamic processes by creating a discrete-time step-by-step model of continuous dynamic processes"; and "A block-based programming language ... to lessen programming difficulties among novice learners". The framework is implemented as a four-step design process applied across three science domains.
requirements: Domain analysis (ECD steps 1-2) must be completed before DSML block creation, identifying target audience, content boundaries, prerequisites, known difficulties, and concept relations
constraints: The design presumes an existing block-based programming environment in which DSML constructs can be embedded
target_learners: elementary, middle, and high school students in K-12 science
target_learning_goals: synergistic learning of STEM domain concepts and computational thinking concepts and practices
examples: Steps 1 and 2 applied ECD to unpack Physics, CT, and computational modeling constructs for a high school kinematics DSML (Table 2, Fig. 3).
key_sources: Nicole M. Hutchins & Gautam Biswas & Ningyu Zhang & Caitlin Snyder & Ákos Lédeczi & Miklós Maróti. (2020). Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00209-z

article_title: An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China
citation: Gretchen Geng · Junyu Chen. (2026). An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers' pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10602-5
title: DST-informed Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) model specifying five knowledge domains
description: The article introduces the DST-informed PCK model, which specifies AI-empowered PCK by detailing the five domains of knowledge teachers draw upon: teaching practice and scaffolding, curriculum knowledge, subject content knowledge, student diversity and inclusive education, and educational contexts. Grounded in Dynamic Systems Theory, it treats PCK as emergent, adaptive, and context-sensitive rather than static, informing teaching practice and scaffolding strategies for personalised student learning.
requirements: Teachers must draw on all five PCK domains for the model to inform teaching practice and scaffolding strategies
constraints: Developed from a small longitudinal study of eight rural language teachers in one Chinese school
target_learning_goals: AI-integrated pedagogical content knowledge
key_sources: Gretchen Geng · Junyu Chen. (2026). An empirical longitudinal study of AI integration in transforming teachers' pedagogical content knowledge: insights from language educators in rural China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10602-5

article_title: Digital storytelling as a disciplinary literacy enhancement tool for EFL students
citation: Chubko, N., Morris, J. E., McKinnon, D. H., Slater, E. V., & Lummis, G. W. (2020). Digital storytelling as a disciplinary literacy enhancement tool for EFL students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09833-x
title: DST as a multimodal middle ground that facilitates community-of-practice formation and shared knowledge construction for EFL students
description: The article frames digital storytelling as an educational technology that "establishes a meaningful and inclusive multimodal learning context" in which EFL students with different life experiences, sociocultural backgrounds and proficiencies negotiate concepts. Drawing on communities-of-practice theory, the authors argue the videomaking process encourages students to construct shared knowledge, gives them autonomy, and creates a context for collaboration, with DST serving as a tool for adapting prior beliefs about STEM-A to a video format. In this study the framework explains why video-producing groups showed the largest disciplinary literacy gains.
requirements: Students work in groups on videomaking tasks tied to inquiry-based astronomy content
Teachers should be ready to enter a community of practice with their students and co-construct disciplinary knowledge
constraints: The mechanism account is the authors' interpretation of a small-sample case study; time spent on video production and group composition varied across groups
target_learners: EFL students aged 10-16 learning STEM content in English
target_learning_goals: Astronomy (STEM-A) disciplinary literacy in English
Conceptual understanding of Moon phases and the Solar System
examples: Kyrgyzstani groups made English videos about planets or Moon phases within the JTST astronomy course; the two Moon-phase video groups showed the steepest SOLO gains
key_sources: Chubko, N., Morris, J. E., McKinnon, D. H., Slater, E. V., & Lummis, G. W. (2020). Digital storytelling as a disciplinary literacy enhancement tool for EFL students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09833-x

article_title: Investigating social vulnerability in children using computer mediated role-play
citation: Fallon, T. L., Aylett, R., Minnis, H. and Rajendran, G. (2018). Investigating social vulnerability in children using computer mediated role-play. Computers and Education, 125, pp. 458-464. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.06.027
title: Theme-matched DSE vignette and Kar2ouche computer role-play assessment tasks
description: A newly created set of 22 theme-matched measures: 11 paper-pencil vignettes and 11 computer-mediated role-play scenarios built in the Kar2ouche story-boarding tool, in which "the child and the researcher role-play by typing into the speech bubbles". Items were independently validated by an expert against DSM-V DSE symptoms on a 5-point rating scale, and both formats were matched on themes and scoring (0–2 per item). Inter-rater reliability was r = .82 for vignettes and r = .99 for the computer task.
requirements: Items must be validated against the specific DSM-V symptoms of Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder
Paper-pencil and computer versions must be matched on themes and scoring to be comparable
constraints: Complete materials are available only by contacting the first author
Scoring of justification questions requires subjective judgement by trained raters
target_learners: typically developing children aged 6, 8 and 10 years
children in middle childhood being assessed for social vulnerability
target_learning_goals: measuring disinhibited social engagement and social vulnerability
assessing social safety awareness and theory of mind
examples: Children completed the tasks individually with a researcher in a quiet room at school, with testing approximately 1 hour per child; presentation order was counterbalanced and pseudo-randomised.
key_sources: Fallon, T. L., Aylett, R., Minnis, H. and Rajendran, G. (2018). Investigating social vulnerability in children using computer mediated role-play. Computers and Education, 125, pp. 458-464. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.06.027

article_title: Digital Storytelling: A Multimodal Narrative Writing Genre
citation: Balaman, S. (2018). Digital storytelling: A multimodal narrative writing genre. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 202-212. http://www.jlls.org
title: Eight-step digital storytelling production sequence embedded in a writing course
description: The article prescribes a reusable lesson/unit sequence for DS-integrated writing: writing and rewriting the narrative in three drafts, storyboarding, selecting suitable multimedia elements and accompanying them with scripts, recording the voice, using WeVideo to make digital stories, in-class presentations, sharing via Facebook, and getting feedback on the videos via Facebook. The sequence keeps the process-writing core while adding multimodal layers and authentic audience feedback.
requirements: A video-editing tool (WeVideo), storyboard sheets, a Google Drive account for lecturer feedback, and a Facebook account for sharing and peer feedback
constraints: Both groups spent the same amount of time (almost 42 hours in total) on the project implementation, with weekly time reducing from five hours to 2 or 3 hours toward the term's end
target_learners: intermediate-level EFL English-major students in preparatory programs
target_learning_goals: narrative paragraph writing
multimodal composition
examples: The experimental group prepared five different digital stories following this procedure on the same topics the control group wrote as traditional narrative paragraphs
key_sources: Balaman, S. (2018). Digital storytelling: A multimodal narrative writing genre. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 202-212. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1193109

article_title: Digital Storytelling: A Multimodal Narrative Writing Genre
citation: Balaman, S. (2018). Digital storytelling: A multimodal narrative writing genre. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 202-212. http://www.jlls.org
title: Integrate digital storytelling into writing instruction only with teacher training, a detailed implementation plan, and continued focus on the writing process
description: The article recommends that teachers adopting DS be cautious because improper utilization can create problems, especially for students with limited access to technology. Teachers "should have training on how to use this application before applying it in the classroom setting", students should be encouraged to focus on the writing process rather than end-products, and teachers or administrators should make a detailed plan covering time, aims, curricular goals, assessment, and equipment before implementation.
requirements: Teacher training on the application before classroom use; a detailed plan indicating needed time, aim, curricular match, assessment issues, and necessary equipment
constraints: Students with limited access to technology and limited experience using it in their real lives may face problems; the implementation may not produce satisfying results if unplanned
target_learners: EFL learners in 21st-century composition classes, including students with limited technology access
target_learning_goals: narrative writing skills
multimodal literacy
examples: The article's own implementation allocated equal weekly writing-course time to both groups and used free tools (WeVideo, Google Drive, Facebook) to reduce access barriers
key_sources: Balaman, S. (2018). Digital storytelling: A multimodal narrative writing genre. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 202-212. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1193109

article_title: Simulation-based training for teaching infection prevention: from realistic to virtual environments.
citation: Souza Raissa Silva; Carvalho Dárlinton Barbosa Feres; Félix Adriana Maria da Silva; Dias Ana Angélica Lima. (2025). Simulation-based training for teaching infection prevention: from realistic to virtual environments. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2024-0288
title: Design Science Research as the guiding paradigm for developing and evaluating educational simulation artifacts
description: Design Science Research (DSR) is described as "a technology-driven problem-solving paradigm that focuses on creating artifacts to address relevant, complex, and contextually grounded challenges". It entails rigorous scientific investigation of the artifact development process together with evaluation of the artifact's suitability and relevance in problem-solving. The study applied six DSR stages: awareness, suggestion, development, iterative evaluation, conclusion, and communication.
requirements: Iterative technological development with low-fidelity prototypes for evaluation in complex application domains
target_learning_goals: Development and evaluation of technology-based learning artifacts
examples: The team created a low-fidelity PowerPoint prototype demonstrating design decisions and artifact performance as a final validation step
key_sources: Souza Raissa Silva; Carvalho Dárlinton Barbosa Feres; Félix Adriana Maria da Silva; Dias Ana Angélica Lima. (2025). Simulation-based training for teaching infection prevention: from realistic to virtual environments. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2024-0288

article_title: Self-efficacy and application of skills in the workplace after multidisciplinary trauma masterclass participation: a mixed methods survey and interview study.
citation: Haverkamp Frederike J. C., Rahim Idris, Hoencamp Rigo, Fluit Cornelia R. M. G., Van Laarhoven Kees J. H. M., Tan Edward C. T. H. (2022). Self-efficacy and application of skills in the workplace after multidisciplinary trauma masterclass participation: a mixed methods survey and interview study. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-022-02159-8
title: Multidisciplinary trauma masterclass combining individual preparation, lectures, small-group case discussions and cadaver and porcine laboratories
description: The DSATC course is a three-day multidisciplinary masterclass combining the surgical and anesthetic trauma care courses. It consists of "individual theoretical preparation (DSTC course manual and recommended articles on anesthesiology) followed by three physical course days filled with lectures, small-group case discussions, and case-based hands-on workshops in the anatomy and operative porcine laboratories". In the porcine laboratory, surgical and anesthesia participants, nurses and faculty work at each operating table on simulated trauma cases, with interdisciplinary collaboration and communication integrated into all working formats.
requirements: Highly experienced specialist faculty trained via a teach-the-teacher course
Cadaver and operative porcine laboratory facilities
Multidisciplinary participant mix at each operating table
constraints: The multidisciplinary integration of the surgical and anesthetic courses is described as a unique feature of the Dutch organizational committee
target_learners: Senior residents and attending physicians in trauma surgery or anesthesiology
target_learning_goals: Self-efficacy in technical and nontechnical trauma skills
Damage control principles
Multidisciplinary teamwork
examples: Faculty members are the only people in the operation room aware of injury locations beforehand, while participants locate, expose and treat the injuries
key_sources: Haverkamp Frederike J. C., Rahim Idris, Hoencamp Rigo, Fluit Cornelia R. M. G., Van Laarhoven Kees J. H. M., Tan Edward C. T. H. (2022). Self-efficacy and application of skills in the workplace after multidisciplinary trauma masterclass participation: a mixed methods survey and interview study. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-022-02159-8

article_title: Dimensionless squared jerk: An objective differential to assess experienced and novice probe movement in obstetric ultrasound.
citation: Dromey BP, Ahmed S, Vasconcelos F, Mazomenos E, Kunpalin Y, Ourselin S, Deprest J, David AL, Stoyanov D, Peebles DM. (2021). Dimensionless squared jerk: An objective differential to assess experienced and novice probe movement in obstetric ultrasound. Prenatal Diagnosis. https://doi.org/10.1002/pd.5855
title: Dimensionless squared jerk (DSJ) metric with electromagnetic probe tracking for ultrasound skill assessment
description: DSJ is a normalised smoothness measure of hand movement, "a derivative of acceleration with respect to time and distance while remaining independent of spurious peaks and dimension". In this study a 6-DOF Aurora electromagnetic sensor on a 3D-printed holder tracked the probe while participants performed BPD, AC and FL biometry on a SPACE-FAN ST phantom; DSJ was computed with the Hogan and Sternad formula using translation only. The setup used clinical ultrasound machines, making it reproducible by other groups.
requirements: Electromagnetic probe tracking hardware attached to a clinical ultrasound probe
A defined task with recorded probe position over time to compute DSJ
constraints: Only translation (3 DOF) was used to compute dimensionless jerk and path length
Validated on a phantom that could not simulate fetal movement, BMI variation or patient-related challenges
target_learners: accredited specialists in training or assessment roles
target_learning_goals: technical psychomotor skill in obstetric ultrasound probe handling
examples: Ten experienced and ten novice sonographers scanned a commercially available second-trimester phantom while probe position was recorded with the Aurora electromagnetic tracking system
key_sources: Dromey BP, Ahmed S, Vasconcelos F, Mazomenos E, Kunpalin Y, Ourselin S, Deprest J, David AL, Stoyanov D, Peebles DM. (2021). Dimensionless squared jerk: An objective differential to assess experienced and novice probe movement in obstetric ultrasound. Prenatal Diagnosis. https://doi.org/10.1002/pd.5855

article_title: A randomised controlled trial of sensory awareness training and additional motor practice for learning scalpel skills in podiatry students.
citation: Causby Ryan S, McDonnell Michelle N, Reed Lloyd, Hillier Susan L. (2016). A randomised controlled trial of sensory awareness training and additional motor practice for learning scalpel skills in podiatry students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0817-8
title: Dynamical systems theory account of scalpel skill learning as integration of afferent, cognitive and efferent systems
description: The article frames scalpel skill learning within dynamical systems theory (DST), under which "voluntary movement involves the interaction of three systems: afferent (sensory), cognitive and efferent (motor)". A motor plan is devised from predictive processes, and while it is executed, sensory feedback loops back into the system, enabling comparison of the resultant and intended plan and subsequent modification. This framework motivated testing whether targeting the sensory (afferent) component via sensory awareness training could improve dexterous motor learning.
requirements: Learning tasks must engage the integrated sensorimotor system; the grip-lift task was chosen because it represents the interaction between afferent and efferent stimuli
constraints: The article notes there is little evidence relating to improving hand function or dexterity via sensory training, with prior systematic reviews mostly not evaluating motor learning or dextrous hand function
target_learners: health profession students learning fine motor clinical skills
target_learning_goals: dexterous use of small tools such as scalpels
integration of sensory feedback into motor planning
examples: The trial operationalised the sensory component as Feldenkrais Awareness Through Movement training, described as an educational system that develops a functional awareness of the self in the environment
key_sources: Causby Ryan S, McDonnell Michelle N, Reed Lloyd, Hillier Susan L. (2016). A randomised controlled trial of sensory awareness training and additional motor practice for learning scalpel skills in podiatry students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0817-8

article_title: Teaching and assessing procedural skills: a qualitative study.
citation: Touchie Claire, Humphrey-Murto Susan, Varpio Lara. (2013). Teaching and assessing procedural skills: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-69
title: Structure procedural skills training around directed self-guided learning with deliberate practice and objective assessment rather than ad-hoc self-direction
description: The article recommends that acquisition and assessment of procedural skills "should move toward a more structured system of teaching, deliberate practice and objective assessment", proposing directed self-guided learning (DSGL) as the means. DSGL creates conditions so that even in unsupervised settings the educator is present through the design and structure of the learning setting, requiring a knowledgeable educator to design practice using validated learning principles. This answers residents' expressed desire for more direction while circumventing limited supervisor availability.
requirements: A knowledgeable educator to design practice conditions using validated learning principles
Opportunities for direct observation and feedback built into the structure
constraints: Complete learner autonomy should not be the ultimate goal of medical education; some level of supervision should be maintained
The recommendation arises from a single-site qualitative study whose perceptions may apply to only one program
target_learning_goals: acquisition and maintenance of procedural skills proficiency
examples: The study's program had no formal procedural skills curriculum; residents logged procedures and received once-yearly mannequin practice through a mandatory two-day critical care course
key_sources: Touchie Claire, Humphrey-Murto Susan, Varpio Lara. (2013). Teaching and assessing procedural skills: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-69
